Series::sensitivity¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::sensitivity() const -> Series

What It Does¶

sensitivity() returns the current reverse-mode sensitivity associated with this Series.

For tracked leaves after a reverse pass, that returned Series is the quantity most people informally call “the gradient.” It has the same logical shape as the source value and stores how the current objective changed with respect to each element of that source.

Read This First¶

sensitivity() always answers one local question:

with respect to this specific Series, what sensitivity is currently stored?

That means the same reverse pass can leave different, equally valid numbers on different nodes.

If y was built from x and you call

y.reverse();

then:

  • x.sensitivity() is dL/dx, which for scalar y is the familiar dy/dx

  • y.sensitivity() is dL/dy, which for scalar y as the objective is usually 1

So when users want “the derivative of the result with respect to the input,” the value they usually mean is read from the tracked input leaf, not from the result node itself.

There is one subtle but important current-surface behavior to keep in mind: when no stored sensitivity exists yet, this method returns a same-shaped zero-valued Series rather than throwing.

That is convenient for printing, but it means you should use has_sensitivity() when you need to distinguish “no stored sensitivity yet” from “a stored sensitivity that happens to be all zeros.”

This method is the read side of the autograd flow. It does not perform any propagation itself.

  • tracks_slope_() decides whether this Series should receive sensitivity as a tracked leaf.

  • reverse() computes and stores that sensitivity.

  • sensitivity() reads whatever is currently stored.

Parameters¶

None.

Returns¶

Series The stored sensitivity, or a same-shaped zero-valued Series when no stored sensitivity currently exists.

Mathematical Meaning¶

If x is a tracked leaf and L is the scalar objective used by reverse(), then x.sensitivity() stores the elementwise quantity

dL/dx

If x is a vector or matrix, the returned Series has the same shape as x, and each position tells you how a small change at that position would affect L.

When reverse-mode was seeded from a non-scalar output y, the effective objective is

L = sum(seed * y)

so the stored sensitivity is really dL/dx, not “the derivative of y” in an unqualified sense.

Where The Stored Result Lives¶

After a computation such as

auto y = f(x);
y.reverse();

there are usually several different derivatives in play.

  • x.sensitivity() answers how the scalar objective changes with respect to x. For a scalar y, that is the familiar dy/dx.

  • y.sensitivity() answers how the scalar objective changes with respect to y itself. When y is the scalar objective, that quantity is usually dL/dy = 1.

So these two reads are not interchangeable:

  • x.sensitivity() is where you usually inspect the derivative you care about in optimization code

  • y.sensitivity() is sensitivity stored on the output node itself

This distinction is the main reason a snippet can appear to “return zero” even when the product rule or chain rule is working correctly underneath.

Shape And Dtype Notes¶

  • the returned sensitivity follows the source shape

  • element positions line up one-for-one with the source positions

  • the result is meant for numeric interpretation, not as a boolean state probe

For boolean existence checks, prefer has_sensitivity().

Examples¶

Example 1. After a reverse pass, sensitivity() returns the stored element-aligned sensitivity.

auto x = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 2.0},
    {3.0, 4.0},
}, pluss::cfg::tracks_slope());

x.mul(3.0).sum().reverse();
std::cout << pluss::series::print(x.sensitivity());

The scalar objective here is

L = sum(3x) = 3x₁₁ + 3x₁₂ + 3x₂₁ + 3x₂₂

so every partial derivative is 3. That is why every entry of the stored sensitivity is 3.

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 3.0000 3.0000 ⎤
⎣ 3.0000 3.0000 ⎦

Example 2. Before any reverse pass has populated one, the current public surface returns zeros.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

std::cout << x.sensitivity();

This is a storage-state quirk, not a mathematical statement that a reverse pass already proved the sensitivity is zero.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 3. Pairing has_sensitivity() with sensitivity() disambiguates that state cleanly.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

std::cout << "has_dL_dx=" << (x.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
std::cout << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

has_dL_dx=false
pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Example 4. Clearing sensitivity resets the stored value so a later reverse pass can populate a fresh one.

auto reuse = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
reuse.tracks_slope_(true);

reuse.mul(2.0).sum().reverse();
std::cout << "first_dL_dx=" << reuse.sensitivity() << "\n";

reuse.clear_sensitivity();
reuse.mul(5.0).sum().reverse();
std::cout << "second_dL_dx=" << reuse.sensitivity() << "\n";

The first objective is L₁ = 2x₁ + 2x₂ + 2x₃, so its stored sensitivity is [2, 2, 2]. After clearing, the second objective is L₂ = 5x₁ + 5x₂ + 5x₃, so the new stored sensitivity is [5, 5, 5].

Output¶

first_dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 2, 2]
second_dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 5, 5]

Example 5. The exact scalar snippet x * x.cos() reads back as zero on y.sensitivity() when the input leaf was never marked for tracking.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.7);
auto y = x * x.cos();

y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "x_has_dy_dx=" << (x.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
std::cout << "y_has_stored_sensitivity=" << (y.has_sensitivity() ? "true" : "false") << "\n";
std::cout << "y_sensitivity=" << y.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

The forward value is

y = x cos(x)

At x = 1.7, that evaluates to -0.21903564030239187.

The important point is not the forward value but the storage destination. reverse() can only populate dy/dx onto leaves that were opted into tracking. Since x was never marked, there is no stored input sensitivity to read back.

Output¶

y=-0.21903564030239187
x_has_dy_dx=false
y_has_stored_sensitivity=false
y_sensitivity=0

Example 6. Once the input is tracked, the same product-rule computation stores dy/dx on x, while the scalar output stores dL/dy = 1.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.7, pluss::cfg::tracks_slope());
auto y = x * x.cos();

y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dy=" << y.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

Here

y = x cos(x)

so the product rule gives

dy/dx = 1·cos(x) + x·(-sin(x))
      = cos(x) - x sin(x)

At x = 1.7:

dy/dx = cos(1.7) - 1.7 sin(1.7) = -1.8146746720647213

Because the reversed objective is the scalar output itself, L = y, the output-node sensitivity is

dL/dy = 1

Output¶

y=-0.21903564030239187
dy_dx=-1.8146746720647213
dL_dy=1

Example 7. Quotient-rule derivatives are read from sensitivity() the same way.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.7);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.div(x.square().add(1.0));
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

The forward function is

y = x / (1 + x²)

Differentiate with the quotient rule:

dy/dx = ((1 + x²)·1 - x·2x) / (1 + x²)²
      = (1 - x²) / (1 + x²)²

At x = 1.7:

dy/dx = (1 - 1.7²) / (1 + 1.7²)² = -0.12490004692012345

Output¶

y=0.43701799485861187
dy_dx=-0.12490004692012345

Example 8. Chain-rule compositions store the full composed derivative on the tracked input.

auto x = pluss::make_series(1.2);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.square().cos();
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

The outer function is cos(u) and the inner function is u = x², so

dy/dx = (-sin(u)) · du/dx
      = -sin(x²) · 2x

At x = 1.2:

dy/dx = -sin(1.2²) · 2(1.2) = -2.3795000356600475

Output¶

y=0.13042370873814554
dy_dx=-2.3795000356600475

Example 9. Hyperbolic and inverse-family methods use the same storage model.

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.25);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.atanh();
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

For

y = atanh(x)

the derivative is

dy/dx = 1 / (1 - x²)

At x = 0.25:

dy/dx = 1 / (1 - 0.25²) = 1.0666666666666667

Output¶

y=0.2554128118829953
dy_dx=1.0666666666666667

Example 10. Special functions also write their derivatives into sensitivity().

auto x = pluss::make_series(0.4);
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.erf();
y.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << y.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dy_dx=" << x.sensitivity().item<double>() << "\n";

For

y = erf(x)

the derivative is

dy/dx = (2 / √π) exp(-x²)

At x = 0.4:

dy/dx = (2 / √π) exp(-0.4²) = 0.9615412988393078

Output¶

y=0.42839235504666845
dy_dx=0.9615412988393078

Example 11. Scalar objectives can target selected positions directly rather than reducing the whole series.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto objective = 2.0 * x.pos(0) + 4.0 * x.pos(1) + x.pos(2).sqrt();
objective.reverse();

std::cout << "L=" << objective.item<double>() << "\n";
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity()) << "\n";

The scalar objective is

L = 2x₁ + 4x₂ + √x₃

Differentiate entry by entry:

dL/dx₁ = 2
dL/dx₂ = 4
dL/dx₃ = 1 / (2√x₃)

At x = [1, 2, 3]:

dL/dx₃ = 1 / (2√3) = 0.28867513459481287

Output¶

L=11.732050807568877
Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 4, 0.28867513459481287]

Example 12. A mixed scalar objective can combine trigonometric, constant-weighted, and logarithmic terms.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto objective = x.pos(0).sin() - 1.5 * x.pos(1).cos() + x.pos(2).log();
objective.reverse();

std::cout << "L=" << objective.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

The objective is

L = sin(x₁) - 1.5 cos(x₂) + log(x₃)

Differentiate each position:

dL/dx₁ = cos(x₁)
dL/dx₂ = 1.5 sin(x₂)
dL/dx₃ = 1 / x₃

At x = [1, 2, 3]:

dL/dx₁ = cos(1) = 0.5403023058681398
dL/dx₂ = 1.5 sin(2) = 1.3639461402385225
dL/dx₃ = 1 / 3 = 0.3333333333333333

Output¶

L=2.56430352829672
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5403023058681398, 1.3639461402385225, 0.3333333333333333]

Example 13. When the scalar objective contains products of subexpressions, the stored sensitivity reflects those internal product-rule terms too.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto objective = x.pos(0).sin() - 1.5 * x.pos(1).cos() * x.pos(2).log();
objective.reverse();

std::cout << "L=" << objective.item<double>() << "\n";
std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

Here

L = sin(x₁) - 1.5 cos(x₂) log(x₃)

The partial derivatives are

dL/dx₁ = cos(x₁)
dL/dx₂ = 1.5 sin(x₂) log(x₃)
dL/dx₃ = -1.5 cos(x₂) / x₃

At x = [1, 2, 3]:

dL/dx₁ = cos(1) = 0.5403023058681398
dL/dx₂ = 1.5 sin(2) log(3) = 1.4984479907474777
dL/dx₃ = -1.5 cos(2) / 3 = 0.2080734182735712

Output¶

L=1.5272470275894714
dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5403023058681398, 1.4984479907474777, 0.2080734182735712]

Example 14. For a non-scalar output, the stored sensitivity belongs to the seeded scalar objective you chose.

auto x = pluss::make_series({1.0, 2.0, 3.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto y = x.mul(x);
y.reverse(pluss::make_series({1.0, 10.0, 100.0}));

std::cout << "dL_dx=" << x.sensitivity() << "\n";

The forward output is

y = [x₁², x₂², x₃²]

The seed defines the scalar objective

L = 1·y₁ + 10·y₂ + 100·y₃
  = 1·x₁² + 10·x₂² + 100·x₃²

So the stored sensitivity is

dL/dx₁ = 1 · 2x₁ = 2
dL/dx₂ = 10 · 2x₂ = 40
dL/dx₃ = 100 · 2x₃ = 600

Output¶

dL_dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, 40, 600]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • sensitivity() is a numeric readout, not a presence check.

  • On the current verified surface, “no stored sensitivity yet” reads back as a zero-valued series instead of an exception.

  • If you need to know whether the value was actually populated by reverse-mode, call has_sensitivity() too.

  • The returned value should always be interpreted relative to the scalar objective that reverse() actually used.

  • y.sensitivity() is not a synonym for “the derivative of y with respect to the inputs.” It is the sensitivity stored on y itself.

  • The exact snippet x = make_series(1.7); y = x * x.cos(); y.reverse(); raises because x was never marked for tracking, so y has no connected graph. Opt x in first (x.tracks_slope_(true) or pluss::cfg::tracks_slope()).

  • A zero-valued readback can therefore mean either “the derivative is actually zero” or “no stored sensitivity exists yet.” Use has_sensitivity() to distinguish those states.

Summary¶

Use sensitivity() to read the current reverse-mode sensitivity in series form. It answers how the scalar objective used by reverse() changes with respect to this specific Series, whether that Series is an input leaf, an intermediate, or the output itself. In practice, most optimization code reads tracked leaves such as x.sensitivity(), and pairs that read with has_sensitivity() whenever presence-versus-zero matters.

See Also¶

  • Series::has_sensitivity: boolean presence test.

  • Series::reverse: populate the stored sensitivity.

  • Series::clear_sensitivity: clear the stored value.
